newsitem.title: FRANCE: France orders Thorn to improve publicity.
newsitem.headline: France orders Thorn to improve publicity.

text.p: France on Sunday ordered British electrical giant Thorn Plc to improve publicity in a new store after charges that its sales pitch could trap poor clients into over-paying for goods in weekly instalments.

"The shop's publicity could be considered insufficient, misleading or deceitful," Finance Minister Jean Arthuis said after a lightning probe by the official consumer watchdog into a new shop in Thorn's rent-to-own Crazy George's chain.
"So they have to change it. Consumers must be clearly informed," he said.

Thorn had agreed to the ministry demands and would close the store in Bobigny, a northern Paris suburb, for several days to carry out the changes, officials said. Advertisments around the shop say: "Choose, pay 10 francs ($2), it's yours!".
The store, the first Crazy George's shop in France, opened on Saturday as part of a planned European expansion by the chain, which has 45 shops in Britain modelled on a successful U.S. formula.

Among Crazy George's offers in France, for instance, is a freezer for 85 francs ($17) a week. Costing 5,987 francs ($1,170) to buy outright, the consumer acquires it only after three years' rental costing 13,260 francs ($2,600).

"If someone tells you you're the owner of a fridge after paying 20 francs ($4) and the contract is not a sales contract but a rental contract with a purchase option, then the advertising is clearly deceitful," Arthuis said earlier.

The Ministry demanded that the cost of renting a product before it belonged to a client be clearly marked on all publicity and that the shop should scrap suggestions that clients were acquiring products on signature of a contract.
Goods can be returned at any time and Crazy George's says the so-called New Buy Scheme enables people with little income to obtain household goods without debt.
The opposition Socialist Party said it was outraged by the Crazy George's system, hitherto untested in France.
"These are shops for poor people where the poor will be paying twice what the rich pay," Socialist Party leader Lionel Jospin said.
"It's a way of exploiting poverty," he said on Saturday night. "This is something really crazy and absurd."
Jospin's charges seemed to touch a raw nerve in France, which is grappling with record unemployment of 12.6 percent, persistent gloom about the economy and wide social inequalities.
